1.text:
How Far Is Too Far?

Welcome back to the speculative science unit! Today's topics come straight out of science fiction: warp drives, Dyson spheres and star travel.

We'll use the Evidence Meter from Deck 21 on the biggest engineering dreams people have ever had. Our question: how far is too far?

2.text:
Are We There Yet?

Guess first: how long would our fastest outbound spacecraft take to reach the nearest star? The answer is 75,000 years for Voyager 1's speed to cover the distance to Proxima Centauri.

Voyager 1 is the fastest probe now leaving the Solar System, at about 17 km/s. ESTABLISHED FACT. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star, is 4.24 light-years away. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Distance ÷ speed gives about 75,000 years. (Voyager isn't aimed at Proxima.) That's arithmetic, so it's an ESTABLISHED FACT. Space is really, really big.

3.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist. Copy these as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can explain why the speed of light is a limit. I can use time dilation to explain GPS and muons. I can trace Voyager's trip out of the heliosphere. I can calculate travel time to the nearest stars. I can judge plans like Breakthrough Starshot. I can compare generation ships, sleep and robots.

I can describe how a warp drive would work on paper. I can explain what the Casimir effect shows. I can explain what a Dyson sphere is and how to spot one. I can weigh Tabby's Star and other "alien" candidates. I can rank civilizations on the Kardashev scale. And I can grade science fiction with the Evidence Meter. These connect to Indiana standards ES.1.5, ES.1.1 and ES.2.2 and NGSS Practices 6 and 7, plus some enrichment.

4.text:
The Cosmic Speed Limit

These are the rules of the road. The speed of light in a vacuum is 299,792 km per second. Nothing with mass can reach the speed of light. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Moving clocks run slow. Muons from cosmic rays reach the ground because of this. They should break down long before they get here, but their clocks run slow. ESTABLISHED FACT. A fast traveler ages less than the people back home. ESTABLISHED FACT.

This isn't just theory. GPS clocks would drift 38 microseconds per day without relativity. Engineers correct for it. Otherwise your phone's map would be off by kilometers within a day.

5.text:
Part 1: Star Travel

What would it really take to reach another star? We'll start with what we've actually done, then look at the best real plans.

Keep this question in mind: could you plan a trip that takes longer than your life?

6.text:
Voyager: Still Going

In 1977, Voyager 1 and 2 launched. ESTABLISHED FACT. In 2004, Voyager 1 crossed the termination shock, where the solar wind slows (94 AU). In 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause into interstellar space (121.6 AU). In 2018, Voyager 2 crossed the heliopause (119 AU). All ESTABLISHED FACT.

In Nov 2026, Voyager 1 is predicted to reach one light-day from Earth. Radio messages will take a full 24 hours to reach it. This is expected from Voyager's well-tracked path, but it has not happened yet, so for now it's a prediction.

And yet, after nearly 50 years, it's less than 0.1% of the way to Proxima. That's arithmetic, an ESTABLISHED FACT.

7.text:
Starshot: Sails Pushed by Lasers

Breakthrough Starshot (2016) proposed tiny chip-sized probes on light sails. ESTABLISHED FACT. Light really pushes sails: Japan's IKAROS sailed on sunlight in 2010. ESTABLISHED FACT.

The plan is for huge lasers on Earth to push the sails to 20% of light speed. INFORMED SPECULATION. At 20% of light speed, Alpha Centauri is about 22 years away. That's arithmetic: ESTABLISHED FACT.

But can a sail survive the laser push and hits from space dust? UNKNOWN.

Did you know? Each sail would be a few meters wide but weigh only about a gram.

8.text:
People or Robots?

Three ways to cross the gap. A generation ship is a slow ship where people live, have kids and die on the way. Only their descendants arrive. INFORMED SPECULATION.

Deep sleep: the crew "hibernates." But humans can't hibernate today; doctors can only cool patients for hours. INFORMED SPECULATION.

Send robots: Voyager has worked in deep space for nearly 50 years with no crew. ESTABLISHED FACT. So think it through: what problems would a generation ship face?

9.text:
Check for Understanding

Do the math. Starshot sails at 20% of light speed. About how long would it take to reach Alpha Centauri, 4.37 light-years away?

Is it A) about 2 years, B) about 22 years, C) about 220 years, or D) about 75,000 years? Show your work: time = distance ÷ speed.

10.text:
Part 2: Warp Drives

Can you beat the speed limit by bending space? Remember from Deck 19: space itself can stretch. Warp drives use the same idea.

If nothing can go faster than light, can space itself?

11.text:
The Alcubierre Warp Drive

In 1994, Miguel Alcubierre found a solution to Einstein's equations: shrink space ahead, stretch it behind. It's math only, but the math is real: ESTABLISHED FACT.

The ship sits still in a "bubble" while space carries it, so it never breaks the local speed limit. INFORMED SPECULATION. It needs negative energy, which normal matter doesn't have. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Early estimates needed more energy than any star makes. Later designs cut this, but not to zero. That's debated, a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. Could a real warp drive ever be built? UNKNOWN.

Did you know? Alcubierre was a physics student and a Star Trek fan when he worked out his warp drive.

12.text:
Negative Energy in the Lab?

In 1997, Steve Lamoreaux measured the Casimir force. Two metal plates very close together get pushed toward each other by the quantum vacuum. ESTABLISHED FACT.

The space between them has slightly less energy than empty space. That's theory-based, but an ESTABLISHED FACT. The effect is tiny: the plates must be less than a millionth of a meter apart. ESTABLISHED FACT.

So "negative energy" isn't pure fantasy. But is there enough for a warp bubble? UNKNOWN.

13.text:
Check for Understanding: Label It

Use the Evidence Meter. "Einstein's equations allow a warp drive, if huge amounts of negative energy exist." What's the best label for building one?

Is it A) established fact, B) plausible hypothesis, C) informed speculation, or D) unknown? Use Slides 11 and 12, and give a reason for your label.

14.text:
Part 3: Megastructures

Would a super-advanced civilization build around its star? This links back to the technosignatures in Deck 23.

How would we spot one from here?

15.text:
Dyson Spheres

A Dyson sphere is a swarm of giant collectors around a star to capture its energy. Freeman Dyson (1960) suggested a huge civilization might do this. INFORMED SPECULATION.

The way to spot one is heat. Anything that absorbs starlight warms up and glows in infrared. ESTABLISHED FACT. So look for stars with too much infrared and too little visible light. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Does any civilization build them? UNKNOWN.

Did you know? Dyson didn't picture a solid shell, which would break apart. He meant a swarm of separate collectors.

16.text:
Alien Megastructures? The Candidates

Odd stars got headlines. Then came the re-checks.

Tabby's Star (2015) dims by up to about 20% at odd times, and that set off "alien megastructure" headlines. But in 2018, scientists found the dimming is deeper in blue than red, which points to dust. A solid panel would block all colors equally. Dust is the best fit: ESTABLISHED FACT.

Project Hephaistos (2024) searched about 5 million stars and found 7 small stars with extra infrared. But follow-ups suggest some may be background galaxies. It's disputed: UNKNOWN.

17.text:
The Kardashev Scale

In 1964, Nikolai Kardashev ranked civilizations by the energy they use. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Type I uses the energy of its whole planet. None known: INFORMED SPECULATION. Type II uses the energy of its whole star, like a full Dyson swarm. INFORMED SPECULATION. Type III uses the energy of its whole galaxy. None were found in about 100,000 galaxies (2015). That's a search result, an ESTABLISHED FACT.

And humanity? We're about 0.73 on Sagan's sliding scale, a rough estimate from world energy use. INFORMED SPECULATION, ROUGH ESTIMATE.

18.text:
How Scientists Hunt for Megastructures

The hunt has five steps. 1, Predict: a warm structure glows in infrared. 2, Search: sky surveys of millions of stars (Gaia, 2MASS, WISE). 3, Rule out: dust disks, young stars and background galaxies. 4, Follow up: sharper images and radio checks. 5, Result: no confirmed megastructure yet.

A clear prediction makes the idea testable. ESTABLISHED FACT. Tabby's Star failed step 3: dust explains it. ESTABLISHED FACT. G-HAT found no galaxy-wide signal in about 100,000 galaxies. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Your turn: what would make you change the label to Established fact?

19.text:
Grade the Movies

Use the Evidence Meter on famous science fiction. Remember, the label is for our verdict, not the movie.

Interstellar (2014): the black hole Gargantua is fictional, but its look was drawn from real equations with physicist Kip Thorne. The black hole is fiction, but the physics behind its look is real. Interstellar also shows time running slower near a black hole. That's real (see GPS), though the amount needs a fast-spinning hole. ESTABLISHED FACT. The Martian (2015): a dust storm tips over a rocket. But Mars air is under 1% as thick as Earth's, so it's too weak. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Star Trek's warp drive is allowed on paper but needs negative energy. INFORMED SPECULATION. Star Wars' loud explosions in space? Space has no air to carry sound. ESTABLISHED FACT.

20.text:
Student Task: Pitch a Starship

Time to plan a real mission. Fill in two parts: A, target star and travel time. B, ship design and Evidence Meter labels.

Pick a target: Proxima Centauri (4.24 ly) or TRAPPIST-1 (about 40 ly). Pick a speed and do the math: time = distance ÷ speed. Crew or robots? Explain how they survive the trip.

Label every part of your plan: EF, PH, IS or UK. The best pitches are honest about which parts are speculation.

21.text:
Exit Ticket

Show what you learned about engineering the impossible.

First, why can't a spaceship simply go faster than light? Second, what has Voyager 1 shown about how far the stars are? Third, what does a warp drive need that we don't have? Fourth, why do scientists look for megastructures in infrared light? Fifth, label it: "A Type II civilization exists in our galaxy."

Then look back at your "I can" list from Slide 3 and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

22.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards, plus one science practice. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.1.1: explain how we study space by observing every kind of light with different telescopes and tools. ES.1.5: show how stars, planetary systems, star clusters, galaxies and galaxy groups fit inside one another, and how big each is.

ES.2.2: describe the objects in the solar system and how it's organized, and know that planets orbit other stars or drift with no star at all. NGSS Science Practice 6: constructing explanations and designing solutions. Use evidence and models to design and test solutions to a problem.
